cards.title: Prospect on Instagram via the Suggested-Accounts Chain
cards.summary: Find copywriting clients on Instagram by qualifying a seed account, then using the suggested-accounts button to chain to similar prospects.
cards.use_when: Sourcing ecommerce brands or info-product clients to write emails, landing pages or ads for, when you need a repeatable prospect list.
steps: Prospect on desktop with many Instagram tabs open; search niche keywords (e.g. 'business coach', 'fitness coach', 'marketing coach') or relevant hashtags to find a first seed account.

Qualify the seed: engaged followers (10k+ rough floor suggested by the source, not a hard rule), optimized bio, link in bio, client results/testimonials in highlights, good view counts. Flag accounts with 100k followers but ~40 views per reel as likely bought followers.
Open the suggested-accounts button to pull a list of related accounts; prospect through that list and repeat recursively.

Engage (follow, like, comment) with qualified accounts until Instagram's algorithm feeds you relevant ads; interact with those ads and mark unrelated accounts 'not interested' to program the feed into a prospecting engine.
Record each qualified prospect in a leads tracking sheet so you can follow up and measure replies.
caveats: Follower threshold is the presenter's heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
Verified badges can be bought, so don't treat them as proof of business quality.
Decide per-account; the source gives signals, not a clean rule.

cards.title: Prospect on YouTube and Build a Swipe Email Account
cards.summary: Mine YouTube for businesses with funnels and email lists, and sign up to their lists from a dedicated 'swipe' inbox.
cards.use_when: Building a target list of store/brand owners to pitch email, landing-page or ad copy, and collecting their live emails as research.
steps: Search YouTube for niche how-to terms (e.g. 'how to make money with real estate') and open channels that look like businesses.
Check for an optimized channel bio, a link in bio, and a video-sales-letter-style intro video — signals of a functioning funnel.
Follow the link and see if it asks for name/email for a free training or lead magnet; that means they run an email list and likely need email copy.
Grab their contact from the channel About page (often info@theirdomain) or from their website.
Create a dedicated 'swipe' email address and sign up to every prospect list with it, so you can study their emails, spot improvement opportunities, and reference specifics in outreach.
caveats: Don't sign up with your primary email; the volume will bury your inbox (the source notes this from experience).
YouTube views are higher-intent than Instagram views per the source, but this is his qualitative claim, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Qualify Prospects on Product Ownership, Offers and Traffic
cards.summary: Judge prospects by owned products, opt-in funnels and real engagement — not by how big their niche is.
cards.use_when: Deciding which ecommerce or info-product businesses to approach for copywriting work, and cutting wasted outreach volume.
steps: Check for engaged followers (not just follower count); a 100k account with ~40 views per reel is a red flag for bought followers.
Confirm they have their own digital product, coaching offer, email list, sales page or opt-in — something copy can improve. Skip prospects whose only monetization is affiliate links/coupon codes.
Check if they're running ads: ad copy is copy, so improving ads, opt-in pages, sales pages and backend email all lift their bottom line, making them viable targets.
Look for evidence of money: paid communities, pricing tiers, sales-call offers ('book a call' = a sales call with a high-ticket program behind it).
Estimate revenue from visible signals (e.g. a community of 343 members at $85/month ≈ $30k/month) to prioritize who's worth your time.
caveats: Revenue estimates from visible numbers are rough, and the source presents them as illustrative, not verified.
Some high-ticket programs sell $6k–$8k, some up to six figures; the source says he's personally seen $15k–$220k packages — treat price ranges as examples, not expectations.

cards.title: Niche-Hop Kills Your Data — Stick With Two to Three Niches
cards.summary: Pick 2–3 niches you know, run one outreach method consistently for at least a month before switching, so you can track a real control.
cards.use_when: Choosing which ecommerce categories or business types to target for copywriting, and structuring outreach tests.
steps: Don't switch niches daily; pick two to three target types, ideally where you already have background knowledge (language, pain points, vocabulary).
Run one outreach approach for at least a month before changing anything; that becomes your control.
Compare months: e.g. month one got five replies; then either test another niche, another outreach method, or another way of finding prospects to try to beat it.
If you've 'run out' of people, rework your leads list and follow up, or try another prospecting platform (Instagram → YouTube → TikTok).
Expect complexity tradeoff: business-to-business niches are harder to enter (you may bomb on early jobs) but more profitable; simpler niches are easier to enter but often less lucrative.
caveats: The source says the niche itself isn't the deciding factor — qualifications of who you target matter more than which niche. He dismisses 'magic untapped niche' guru claims.
One month is the source's minimum consistency window, not a universal law.

cards.title: Position as a Problem Solver, Not an Email Writer
cards.summary: One copywriter who offers 'emails' gets turned down; the one who asks what the business needs and offers the matched service closes more.
cards.use_when: Framing your pitch to an ecommerce brand or info-product business so your offer fits their gap (ads, welcome sequences, landing pages, SMS).
steps: Stop leading with a fixed deliverable ('I do emails'). Ask what they need first, then shape your offer around the answer.
Learn adjacent skills — funnel building, landing page creation, email marketing, welcome sequences, SMS — so you can say yes to what's actually broken.
Build an offer match: if they need content, offer content and email; if they need a funnel, offer a funnel plus a sales page.
Anchor your value in their deficiency, not your preference: 'you're doing X, that's leaving money on the table — here's the fix.'
Watch wins from peers as evidence of ranges (e.g. a $3k/mo retainer, a $1,750/mo retainer bundling 12 emails, 4 YouTube scripts and 30 tweets) — copy the structure, not the exact price.
caveats: These are the source's students' wins, presented as examples, not guaranteed results.
Adding skills also happens on the job — the source says he learned B2B by doing it and initially underperformed.

cards.title: Give Value Before You Ask for the Call
cards.summary: Business owners don't take calls with strangers; send a piece of finished value (emails, teardown) first to buy 15 minutes.
cards.use_when: Reaching out to ecommerce or brand owners to get a conversation that opens the possibility of paid copy work.
steps: Make the thing before you ask: write sample emails, a headline and lead, or a mini-teardown for the specific prospect.
Send it with a low-pressure close: 'here's some work I did for you — if it's useful, let's talk about getting you more wins.'
Don't ask for a call first; the ask is a byproduct of demonstrated value.
Track how many of these value-first outreaches convert to replies and calls so you can improve the message.
Use your skills to make the value actually good — the source says the better the value, the more calls and opportunities.
caveats: The shown win (a large owner replying that he usually ignores such emails) is one anecdote, not a rate.
Give value in a form the business can immediately use, not general praise or promises.

cards.title: Proof Beats Promises in Outreach
cards.summary: Overpromising and free-work offers read as desperate; testimonials, results and borrowed authority do the closing.
cards.use_when: Writing outreach copy to a store/brand owner who gets pitches daily and is deciding whether to trust you.
steps: Stop offering to work for free or guaranteeing money/clients — the source says it makes you look needy and repels buyers.
Assemble proof: screenshots from an email platform, client testimonials, before/after results, or borrowed authority (someone credible vouching for you).
Put proof in the outreach itself, not just your bio, and lead with what you did for someone similar.
Practice showing proof in your earliest pieces of copy so it's natural when it matters.
Pair one piece of proof with the value you already gave them; the source frames it as proof weighing against a thousand pounds of promise.
caveats: 'One ounce of proof equals 1,000 pounds of promise' is the source's metaphor, not a measured conversion rule.
If you have no client proof yet, use sample work and third-party research as your stand-in — don't fabricate testimonials or results.

cards.title: The PP&V Framework for a Copywriting Portfolio
cards.summary: Build a portfolio with Polish, Proof and Variety to raise perceived value and cut perceived risk for a hiring business.
cards.use_when: Assembling or repackaging your portfolio to pitch an ecommerce or info-product business on email, landing page or ad copy.
steps: Polish: revise every piece after feedback. The source says copy isn't polished until you've run it through AI and had it reviewed by peers; rewrite and tighten before showing it.
Proof: include platform screenshots, testimonials or performance numbers where you have them, so a prospect can see the work performed.

Variety: include more than emails — a headline and a 'lead' (the top third of a landing page), a short scroll-stopping explanation of how the product works, and a video sales letter sample. You don't need a whole landing page.
Curate, don't dump: a portfolio is a collection of best work used to increase perceived value and decrease perceived risk, so the pieces should be your strongest, not everything you've written.
Include unpaid sample work — the source says your copy doesn't need to be paid or client work to earn a portfolio spot.
caveats: The source is emphatic that this is a beginner-to-client bridge, not a substitute for doing the work. Portfolio alone doesn't guarantee clients.
Use real screenshots/testimonials only; don't invent metrics.

cards.title: Use Instagram as Your Website
cards.summary: Your profile is your sales page and business card; polishing it beats building a website prospects won't click.
cards.use_when: Setting up or cleaning up your profile before pitching ecommerce or info-product owners.
steps: Treat the profile as the storefront: clear face photo, a positioning name (e.g. 'Marketing Systems' rather than just 'copywriter'), and a bio that says what you do and for whom.
Fill the grid with relevant signals: client results, reels about business, high-value authority photos, social proof and testimonials.
Skip building a website as the primary proof artifact — prospects check Instagram anyway, and sending a link adds friction and looks sketchy.
When you outreach, the profile does the pre-selling so the reply rate improves; the source contrasts an empty/blank profile (ignored) with a dialed-in one (replied to).
Refresh outcomes and testimonials as you accumulate them so the profile grows with your proof.
caveats: This is the source's advice for Instagram-first client acquisition; a site may still be needed for some buyers, so it's a situational call, not absolute.
Don't overstate results or post fabricated wins — the source's whole frame is that consistency between cover and book matters.

cards.title: The Six-Step Client Acquisition Loop
cards.summary: A repeatable sequence: find clients, approach them, give value, call, offer, close.
cards.use_when: Structuring a systematic outreach effort to ecommerce and info-product businesses instead of ad-hoc pitching.
steps: Find clients: build a qualified list (see prospecting cards).
Approach clients: use an outreach message that leads with value.
Give value: deliver something specific before the call.
Call them: get on a call with genuine curiosity, not desperation.
Give them an offer: shape it around what they said they need.
Close them: use proof and a clear next step, then keep the client and hunt for the next.
caveats: The source warns the sequence only works if you actually have the copy skills behind it — outreach without skills won't close.
The source presents 60 days as his own 'gun to my head' plan for replacing a job, not a promise. He says he's seen it happen faster.

cards.title: Treat the Call as Curiosity, Not a Sale
cards.summary: Get on calls to find out if you can help, not to force a close — desperation derails you and repels buyers.
cards.use_when: Running a discovery or sales call with a store or brand owner about copy/email/funnel work.
steps: Drop the 'this is my big break' mindset before the call; the source says it derails you and shows through.
Lead with genuine curiosity: ask what their goals are, what's holding them back, and what they actually need.
Listen for the problem you can solve, then build the offer around what they name — not around what you're best at.
Determine whether you can help; if you can, propose it; if not, don't force it.
Let value exchange and proof do the persuasion, so you don't need to overpromise or discount to win the deal.
caveats: The source says this mindset is more effective, but he presents it as his approach, not a tested conversion benchmark.
Curiosity doesn't replace preparation: you still need relevant proof and skill to back up the offer.

cards.title: Onboarding vs Outreach: Why Both Signals Are Needed
cards.summary: Referrals and inbound profile messages happen only after results — treat them as a byproduct of doing great work, not a starting tactic.
cards.use_when: Planning how to acquire ecommerce clients and understanding where referrals fit in the pipeline.
steps: Don't wait for referrals or inbound messages when starting — build the list and outreach first.
Deliver results on a first client to unlock referrals: the source shows a student's client referring a fitness influencer with 80k+ followers for a funnel build.
Inbound does happen once you're visible: e.g. an optimized profile brought a prospect who reached out directly, leading to $1.2k per high-performing reel.
Use the first client as a case study for the portfolio and for proof in later outreach.
Keep prospecting while serving clients — one client should become two, two should become four, per the source's compounding framing.
caveats: The listed referral and inbound wins are students' anecdotes, not guarantees.
The source is emphatic that none of it works without the underlying copy skill; do the work first.

cards.title: Track Outreach Numbers or You're Playing Blindfolded
cards.summary: Track which messages, niches and platforms produce replies so you can optimize instead of hoping for luck.
cards.use_when: Running any outreach campaign to ecommerce businesses and wanting to know what's actually working.
steps: Start small: track a few basic metrics first to build the habit, then add more as you go.
Keep one outreach approach and one niche stable for at least a month so the numbers mean something (a control).
Log each attempt: who you contacted, which platform, which message, and whether you got a reply.
Compare periods and change one variable at a time (message, niche, or platform) so you know what drove the change.
Treat tracking as a multiplier: the source says just measuring a metric often brings attention and improvement by default.
caveats: Sample sizes from a single month of outreach are tiny; one great client on a third outreach happened, but the source warns that doesn't remove the need to track and keep going.
Numbers here are personal records, not benchmarks to hit.

cards.title: Bias Toward Action: Ready, Fire, Aim
cards.summary: Efficiency of time matters more than total available time; doing beats endless consuming.
cards.use_when: Getting a first client while working a full-time job or studying, or pushing through fear to actually send outreach.
steps: Accept that everyone has time constraints; the source says he worked 80+ hours/week across three jobs and still did the work through efficiency, not extra hours.
When you know the next step, do it immediately instead of re-consuming content — the source frames endless course-watching as 'aiming' that never fires.
Take action while scared; permission to be bad early is part of the process ('you don't have to be great to start').
After acting, use the result to adjust — ready, fire, aim, rather than ready, aim, fire.
Complete the concrete first tasks: write your first piece of copy, set up the profile, join the community, build the list — not just watch the videos.
caveats: The 80+ hours/week and quitting-in-60-days details are the presenter's personal history, not a required path.
Action without skill still won't close clients — the source pairs action with completing the copy fundamentals.

cards.title: The Oversaturation Myth and the Pipie Fallacy
cards.summary: Copywriting is a small, less-crowded online income category; plentiful competition is not fierce competition.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether it's worth entering a crowded-looking category or skipping niches because 'everyone's doing it'.
steps: Compare search interest across online-income routes: the source shows Google Trends with affiliate marketing and dropshipping far above freelance copywriting, which is a tiny line near the bottom.
Reframe competition: a huge number of businesses online hire copywriters, so competitors aren't literally taking your food.

Apply the 100m-dash thought experiment: against 10 Olympic athletes you lose; against 10 (or 10 million) toddlers you win because of the massive skill advantage — so the audience size doesn't decide it, your relative skill does.
Do the things others skip: the source cites analytics showing only ~2% finished his prior 4-hour course, so completion and execution already narrow the field.
Pair this with real outreach, since skill plus outreach is what produces the results he cites.
caveats: The 2% completion figure is from one specific course's analytics, not a general statistic.
Google Trends compares search interest, not market revenue or hiring volume — the source uses it rhetorically.

cards.title: Pick Niches by Opportunity, Not Guru Secrets
cards.summary: No niche is magic; some are harder to enter but more profitable, and any niche works if prospects are qualified.
cards.use_when: Choosing an ecommerce category or client type to focus copywriting outreach on.
steps: Reject 'untapped niche' claims from paid courses — the source says there's no secret niche and he doesn't recommend buying into that framing.

Start from a list of niches you know copywriters are paid well in, then filter for ones you already understand; the source names business coaching/coaching offers and real estate coaching as his own entry points.
Don't niche-hop just because someone in a wins screenshot is in a niche — pick and commit for at least a month (see the consistency card).
Accept rate-of-entry vs profitability tradeoff: B2B is harder to learn (you may bomb early) but more profitable, and you can learn on the job.

Occasionally work outside your niche when an opportunity shows up — the source says he's written for odd niches (e.g. holistic health for over-40s) and that copywriting is copywriting once you know the research.
caveats: The 'business coaching' niche recommendation is the source's personal success story, not a universal best niche.
His prices and high-ticket numbers are examples from his experience, not benchmarks.

cards.title: Do All the Steps — the Secret Is Execution
cards.summary: Everyone knows the steps; the differentiator is doing every one of them instead of asking what you can skip.
cards.use_when: Structuring your own client-acquisition plan and resisting the temptation to shortcut the fundamentals.
steps: Follow the recipe in order: fundamentals first, then outreach, then secondary skills, then AI acceleration.
Don't ask 'what can I get away with not doing' — the source says do all of it; that's what separates the 2% who finish from the rest.
Keep the sequence explicit: find, approach, give value, call, offer, close, then compound with retained clients.
Layer secondary skills (funnels, landing pages, email/SMS sequences) so your offers are broader and AI-resistant.
Use action-step checklists (a copy starter kit) to make sure nothing was skipped rather than relying on memory.
caveats: This is the presenter's philosophy and course structure, not an empirically validated curriculum.
Skipping the fundamentals isn't framed as a shortcut here — the source treats it as the cause of confusion downstream.

cards.title: Referrals as a Client Acquisition Channel
cards.summary: One good result turns into more clients via referrals — build the funnel and let happy clients introduce similar ones.
cards.use_when: Growing an ecommerce copywriting practice after landing a first client, instead of only cold outreach.
steps: Deliver strong results on your first client so referrals become possible.
When a client offers or receives an intro (e.g. 'this is JD, he's looking for a funnel'), treat it as a warm lead and follow up immediately.
Use each referral to broaden the services you offer — the source's example referral led to funnel work, not just copy.
Keep the referral loop going by re-checking in with satisfied clients about who else needs the same work.
Record referral sources in your tracking sheet so you can see which clients and channels generate warm leads.
caveats: Referrals are a consequence of results, not a strategy you can start with before you have any clients.
The 80k-follower referral example is a specific student's story, not a typical outcome.

cards.title: Rate of Entry vs Profitability in Niche Selection
cards.summary: Harder niches pay more but take longer to learn — decide whether to trade entry difficulty for profit.
cards.use_when: Deciding which verticals to pitch for copy/email/funnel work and how much ramp-up you're willing to absorb.
steps: Identify where your chosen niche sits on the difficulty/profit spectrum: business-to-business and finance are usually harder to enter but more profitable; consumer niches are easier to enter but often less lucrative.
Accept that early jobs in a hard niche may go worse while you learn the language (e.g. lead magnets, deliverability, offers) — the source says he 'kind of bombed' early B2B copy.
Once you learn the vocabulary and mechanics, expect a defensible position described by the source as a 'blue ocean for beginners' — harder to enter but better paid.
Use niches where you already have knowledge to speed up research; you know the pain points, terms, and language.
If a good opportunity appears outside your chosen niche, take it anyway; research ability transfers.
caveats: The 'blue ocean' framing is the presenter's interpretation of his own experience, not market data.
Difficulty and profitability are tendencies, not rules — the source says no niche is inherently more profitable than another.
